market_context: United States/general English; USDA composition and equal 1-ounce portions
title: Almonds vs. walnuts: nutritional differences

seo.title: Almonds vs. walnuts: protein, fiber, fat and omega-3
seo.meta_description: Per ounce, almonds provide more protein, fiber and vitamin E; walnuts provide much more polyunsaturated fat and ALA omega-3. Compare the numbers.
seo.search_intent: Compare almonds and walnuts in equal servings and identify the nutritional differences that actually matter.

excerpt: In a 1-ounce serving, almonds provide about 164 calories, 6 g of protein and 3.5 g of fiber; walnuts provide about 185 calories, 4.3 g of protein and 1.9 g of fiber. Walnuts, however, provide roughly 2.5 g of ALA omega-3, while almonds are far richer in vitamin E. Neither wins every category.
content_html:
Almonds and walnuts sit in the same grocery aisle and share the same typical serving size, but their nutrition is not a small variation on the same nut. Almonds contain more protein, fiber and vitamin E; walnuts have a much more polyunsaturated fat profile and provide ALA omega-3.

Equal 1-ounce serving comparison

NutrientAlmonds 1 ozWalnuts 1 oz
Calories~164~185
Protein~6 g~4.3 g
Total fat~14 g~18.5 g
Fiber~3.5 g~1.9 g
Monounsaturated fat~9 g~2.5 g
Polyunsaturated fat~3.5 g~13 g
ALA omega-3Trace~2.5 g

The calorie gap is only about 20 calories per serving, much less dramatic than comparing 579 calories per 100 g of almonds with 654 per 100 g of walnuts.

For protein and fiber, almonds lead

Almonds provide roughly 1.7 g more protein and about 1.6 g more fiber per ounce. Relative to walnuts, that is around 40% more protein and close to twice the fiber.

That does not make almonds a protein equivalent to meat, fish or legumes; it simply makes them more protein-dense within this comparison.

For ALA omega-3, walnuts are in another category

One ounce of walnuts provides roughly 2.5 g of alpha-linolenic acid. Almonds provide very little.

ALA is an essential omega-3, but it is not EPA or DHA. The body converts only a limited portion to these longer-chain forms.

Monounsaturated versus polyunsaturated

Almond fat is dominated by monounsaturated oleic acid—about 9 g per serving. Walnuts are dominated by polyunsaturated fat, with roughly 13 g per ounce.

Both profiles are mostly unsaturated; they are different, not opposites.

Vitamin E creates another large difference

One ounce of almonds provides around 7 mg of vitamin E. Walnuts provide much less alpha-tocopherol, the form used for the vitamin E requirement.

If vitamin E is the specific target within nuts, almonds are far more concentrated.

Walnuts need slightly more storage care

Their high polyunsaturated-fat content makes walnuts more susceptible to oxidation and rancidity. Heat, light and oxygen speed the process.

Both nuts benefit from airtight storage, but walnuts especially benefit from cool storage or refrigeration when kept for longer periods.

So which is better?

For protein, fiber and vitamin E: almonds. For ALA omega-3 and a more polyunsaturated fat profile: walnuts. A varied diet can use both instead of turning a real nutritional difference into an unnecessary either-or decision.

Either serving is still a concentrated food at roughly 160–190 calories, so portion size matters more than declaring an absolute winner.

faq.question: Which has more protein, almonds or walnuts?
faq.answer: Almonds: about 6 g per ounce versus roughly 4.3 g in walnuts.

faq.question: Which has more omega-3?
faq.answer: Walnuts, with about 2.5 g of ALA per ounce. Almonds provide only very small amounts.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Almonds: about 3.5 g per ounce versus roughly 1.9 g in walnuts.
